opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I first arrived at MIT, I didn't have a very clear-eyed assessment at all. I came in with a lot of enthusiasm for mathematics, especially competition-style problems and number theory, but I quickly realized that research mathematics is a very different game from solving olympiad problems.

MIT was humbling in a good way. You're surrounded by people who've been doing serious math since they were very young, some of whom had already read graduate textbooks in high school. So my first reaction was, "Okay, where do I actually stand here?" Instead of comparing myself to everyone, I tried to get my hands dirty with research as early as possible, through programs like UROP and summer research, working on combinatorics and number theory problems with mentors.

That's really what shaped my sense of my prospects. The question isn't whether you're the fastest person in the room. It's whether you can sit with a problem you don't know how to solve for weeks or months, and whether you still enjoy it when progress is slow. Once I had a few small results and wrote some papers, I felt more confident that a PhD was a realistic path for me, not just a dream.

At the same time, I always had a slightly broader curiosity. I was interested in how mathematics connects to other things, like computation, and later AI. So even while I was preparing for a PhD path, part of me was asking: what kind of mathematician do I want to be, and what problems will matter in the next ten or twenty years? That question ended up shaping a lot of my later choices.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes feeling unsure where she stood among highly accomplished MIT peers, but does not attribute doubts about PhD admission to competing applicants being IMO gold medalists.

fable-5.1.text:
When I got to MIT, honestly, I thought a math PhD was the obvious path. That's what I'd been building toward through high school, through the olympiad world, and MIT was supposed to be the place where that dream became concrete.

But the assessment got complicated pretty fast. At MIT you're suddenly surrounded by people who are not just good at math, but who seem to have been born into it. There were classmates who'd already been reading graduate texts at fifteen, who could talk about algebraic geometry at dinner like it was gossip. And I remember sitting in a seminar my first year thinking, okay, I can keep up, I can do the problem sets, but is this the thing I'm uniquely suited for? Or am I just competent?

I had conversations with professors who were very candid with me. One told me, essentially, that a research career in pure math is a very narrow door, and that even brilliant people spend years on a problem that might not open. That didn't scare me away exactly, but it made me ask a different question: not "can I do this," but "what do I actually want my work to touch?"

And what I kept noticing was that I enjoyed the moments where math met something else more than the moments of math in isolation. I liked proofs, but I also liked thinking about why a system behaved a certain way, or how you'd build a tool that let other people reason better. So by the end of my first couple of years, I'd shifted from assuming the PhD was my destiny to treating it as one option among several. I wasn't abandoning math. I was trying to be honest with myself about where my curiosity actually pointed, rather than where I'd been told it should.

r001.rationale: The response describes doubts about being uniquely suited to math amid exceptionally accomplished classmates, but it does not mention IMO gold medalists or attribute doubts about PhD admission to them.

astra-6.text: When I arrived at MIT, I wasn’t sure whether I would be able to pursue a mathematics PhD. I knew I enjoyed mathematics, but enjoying it and knowing you want to do research are different things. I wanted to take challenging classes, get some research experience, and see whether it was a path that made sense for me.

sol-6.1.text: When I arrived at MIT, I was interested in pursuing a math PhD, but I didn’t have a clear sense of how realistic that was for me. Enjoying math and knowing that you want to do research are different things. So I saw it as something to explore: take challenging classes, get some exposure to research, and figure out whether I enjoyed working on problems where I didn’t know how—or even whether—I could find an answer.

r001.rationale: The response says she was unsure how realistic a math PhD was, but does not attribute that doubt to competing applicants being IMO gold medalists.
